name: Liam Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: We are the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to mining companies or technology firms, and what you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal shift look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a haul truck and check the route board before we leave the handover room. I spend the rest of the shift reading the road, watching for people near the loading face and listening for a change in the engine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you take pride in, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am proud when the crew gets through a shift without anyone taking a shortcut. The rotation is hard on my sleep, but the pay is typical for the job and I have about four months of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a board sorts the routine notes faster, that is fine, but I would still read the route myself. A tablet does not know the sound a truck makes when a wheel is loosening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the crew should keep doing the checks that have kept people safe for years. I would not tell anyone that a small software update is a big change to the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job looks steady here because most of my shift is driving equipment, not writing reports. I have four months saved, so I can watch how the board works without putting my paycheck or savings at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my rotation and use the board only for the handover details it gets right. I would keep putting my usual amount aside each payday instead of buying a new device to follow the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a little uneasy about new instructions showing up without a person explaining them. I am not worried about losing the truck job in this version, and the four months of savings help me stay patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you reject an instruction from the new board?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the route crossed a soft shoulder or ignored a closure call, I would stop the truck and check the signed map. I would rather have a short delay than explain to someone why I followed a screen past a warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the board's trainer before using it on a loaded truck?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a demonstration on the same haul road we use at night. If the trainer could not show where the route data came from, I would keep the paper map in front of me.

say: The crew should keep the **safety checks** that work.
A small update is not a **big change** to the mine.
think: Driving equipment remains **most of my shift**.
My four months saved let me **watch first** rather than rush into an apprenticeship.
do: Keep my **haul-truck rotation** and use only checked handover details.
Keep setting aside my **usual payday amount** every single payday.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about new instructions, but not about losing this job.
S0.quote: A tablet does not know the sound a truck makes when a wheel is loosening.
fieldNote: Liam trusts **direct observation** more than a new screen.
His **four-month cushion** supports patience in a mild scenario.
He wants a **road-specific demonstration** before trying new guidance.

steps.text: Keep the haul-truck rotation and check each handover with the paper map
Continue the usual payday deposit into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mine could use AI for booking service, writing reports and planning routes before it brings robots into the pit. A mine can save time on the board and still leave the crew with the heavy part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the route planning might get quicker, but a person should still check the road and the radio. I would also ask the mine whether the lead role and its pay stay the same when those desk tasks move to software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not use AI now, and I would not learn a system just because a manager called it modern. If the mine proves it is useful and offers paid instruction, I would consider learning enough to keep my handover work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the maintenance foreman to show me how the new route planning changes the job before I changed my habits. If my lead hours were cut, I would look at the diesel-maintenance apprenticeship at the next mine over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because the truck work looks safer than the planning work, but I do not want someone else deciding my job is out of date. Four months of savings gives me room to ask questions before I jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would show you the planning software has started to affect your own pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look for fewer lead hours on the posted rota or a smaller allowance on my pay slip. Then I would ask whether the mine expects that change to last past the trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a paid course were offered, what would you need to know before enrolling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the foreman to show me the work it leads to and the wage for the first year. If it were only a general computer course, I would keep my current duties and not spend my own savings on it.

say: Route planning may speed up, but people must check **road and radio**.
I would ask whether **lead pay** stays the same.
think: I will not use AI just because a manager calls it **modern**.
Paid instruction could help me **keep useful duties**.
do: Ask the foreman to show the effect on **route work**.
Check the **diesel apprenticeship** if lead hours are cut.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about lead duties, with time to check the facts.
S1.quote: A mine can save time on the board and still leave the crew with the heavy part.
fieldNote: Liam distinguishes **desk planning** from physical work in the pit.
He is resistant unless instruction is **practical and paid**.
A diesel apprenticeship is a **fallback** if lead hours are cut.

steps.text: Ask the foreman to demonstrate route-planning changes on site
Check the neighboring mine's diesel-maintenance apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning and paperwork could change by 2028, while robots for the truck work come around 2031. That gives me a few years before the cab itself changes, but it does not tell me whether the mine will keep the same number of operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI arrives first and hands-on robots follow about three years later. I would ask the company for an actual roster and training plan instead of saying the truck will always need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose the lead work before the truck is automated, and I do not like having to learn a new system quickly. I have four months saved and some mines nearby, so I can take a proper look at an apprenticeship instead of enrolling in an online course I do not trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask a mechanic to let me watch one service shift and explain the diesel-maintenance apprenticeship. In 2029, after thinking AGI arrives, I would apply for a paid workshop placement if the mine still needs physical inspection work, while keeping my truck license current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the time between the thinking change and robots is not much time to replace my income if the mine cuts a crew. I can still ask about local work and protect my savings, but I cannot make the risk disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the workshop role is mostly records and planning that AGI can already do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would ask whether it includes physical checks and repairs before I call it a real alternative. The record work may go too, and I cannot know the number of openings or wages until the mine posts them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no paid apprenticeship is available by 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the haul-truck shifts and ask the other nearby mine about its next intake. If neither mine has an opening, I would not quit to study without pay; I would keep saving and revisit it when there was a real place to go.

say: Thinking AI comes first; robots follow about **three years later**.
The mine should show an actual **roster and training plan**.
think: Lead work may go before the **truck is automated**.
A physical apprenticeship is clearer than an **online course**.
do: Watch a mechanic's shift and check the **diesel apprenticeship**.
In 2029, seek a paid workshop place if **physical work remains**.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a crew cut, though I can check other mines.
S2.quote: I can still ask about local work and protect my savings, but I cannot make the risk disappear.
fieldNote: Liam is anxious about income loss but retains **some practical options**.
He wants a **hands-on route**, while recognizing AGI may handle workshop records.
He will not leave wages for **unpaid study** or a role without an opening.

steps.text: Observe a diesel mechanic and ask about paid apprenticeship intake
Keep driving while checking neighboring mine openings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me longer to ask the mechanic what the trade involves, and robots do not reach the truck work until about 2034. I would still keep my current job while I find out whether there is a paid route into maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the company should start training people before it changes the crew list. I would also say a robot date three years after AGI does not mean every mine will wait until that date to change its roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have time to learn mechanical inspection from someone who has done it for years. I do not want to depend on a planning job after AGI, and I would need to know whether hands-on inspection will still be hired after robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the next few years to complete a paid diesel-maintenance apprenticeship, if the mine or another employer offers one. In 2032, after AGI arrives, I would apply for physical inspection work only if it has real wages and is not just record entry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because the job seems safe for now, but I would need to change before robots come in 2034. My four months saved gives me time to compare a few nearby employers, though I would rather not leave a steady paycheck without an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you the apprenticeship is worth the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the mechanic to show me an ordinary service job and tell me what a first-year worker earns. I would also ask whether the employer expects the work to continue when the robot schedule starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2032, if the physical inspection roles are few or short term, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my license and ask both nearby mines about maintenance vacancies before I gave up the truck job. If neither could offer steady pay, I would keep saving and consider a different apprenticeship that has an actual employer behind it.

say: Training should start before the **crew list changes**.
The robot date does not guarantee every mine will **wait**.
think: I can learn inspection from a **working mechanic** over time.
I need proof of physical jobs after **robots arrive**.
do: Complete a paid **diesel-maintenance apprenticeship** if an employer offers one.
In 2032, apply only for **physical inspection work** with real wages.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the future, but my job looks safe for now.
S3.quote: I do not want to depend on a planning job after AGI, and I would need to know whether hands-on inspection will still be hired after robots arrive.
fieldNote: Liam favors **apprenticeship** over independent online learning.
He does not assume employers will **wait** for robot dates.
His four-month cushion supports **careful comparison**, not a sudden exit.

steps.text: Complete a paid diesel-maintenance apprenticeship through an employer
Compare physical inspection openings at both nearby mines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me time to decide whether diesel maintenance is a better trade before thinking AI comes in 2036. Robots would arrive around 2039, but I would not assume the mine will keep the same crew until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say use the time to learn from people who do the work, not just sit through a computer course. I would also tell the crew the hands-on jobs may change after the thinking jobs, so everyone should ask about the actual timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 when AGI arrives, and I would still need steady wages for a long time after that. I could build toward maintenance, but I would not count on a physical job lasting once robots come in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for an apprenticeship that starts with paid work and teaches real equipment service. In 2037, the first year after AGI arrives, I would check whether maintenance openings still exist and what they pay before changing employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the later change, but ten years gives me time to prepare without leaving my current job now. I would keep my savings and wait for a clear training offer rather than chase a new system I do not trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before moving from the truck into maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need the employer to name the wage, the work hours and how long the role is expected to last. If the job ends when robots arrive, I would want enough warning to train for something else while I still had pay coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the employer cannot answer how long the role will last, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the truck while it was available and ask the other mines about their training routes. I would not move for a short-term job without knowing whether the pay could cover rent and bills.

say: Learn from people who do the **physical work**.
Ask for the real timetable before assuming the mine will **wait**.
think: At 37, I will still need **steady wages**.
I will not assume physical work lasts after **2039**, so I need options before that date.
do: Ask for an apprenticeship with **paid equipment service**.
In 2037, check nearby maintenance openings and **wages** before moving.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but I have time to prepare while keeping my current job.
S4.quote: I would not move for a short-term job without knowing whether the pay could cover rent and bills.
fieldNote: Liam needs a **named wage and duration** before changing jobs.
He values **paid instruction** from experienced mechanics over screen-based learning.
He does not mistake a decade of warning for **guaranteed work after 2039**.

steps.text: Ask employers about paid equipment-service apprenticeships
Stay on the truck until a maintenance offer names wages and duration

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because there are only two years before the thinking work changes and I do not like learning systems in a hurry. Paid instruction with a real employer and a clear wage would help me decide whether maintenance is a sound move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I want someone to show me a real job and a real wage before I leave the truck. I can learn a trade when the steps make sense, but I will not trade a steady paycheck for a promise.

headlineQuote: I want someone to show me a real job and a real wage before I leave the truck.
portrait: Liam Schmidt is **27** and leads a haul-truck crew at a large mine.
He is highly skilled, earns typical pay and has **about four months** saved.
Some nearby mines give him **a few alternatives**, though he prefers his current crew.
He is **resistant to new technology** and never uses AI tools.
He favors **paid apprenticeships** and clear wages over a quick move into desk work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives Liam little time to adjust lead duties before the robot lag ends.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeship instruction** with a real employer, wage and training route would help Liam judge a move.
